subject: Pathology
vignette: A 62-year-old man with a long history of untreated essential hypertension undergoes echocardiography, which shows marked thickening of the left ventricular wall with a reduced left ventricular cavity. A biopsy shows enlarged cardiomyocytes with large, boxcar-shaped nuclei and abundant cytoplasm, but the total number of nuclei per high-power field is unchanged. The patient later develops heart failure.
question: Which of the following best describes the cellular adaptation responsible for the ventricular wall thickening in this patient?

options.text: An increase in cell number driven by proliferation of resident stem cells
A decrease in tissue mass produced by ubiquitin-proteasome degradation of cytoskeleton
An increase in cell size caused by increased structural proteins and organelles
Replacement of myocardium by a cell type better able to tolerate the pressure load
Disordered precancerous growth of myocytes with pleomorphism and loss of orientation

explanation_correct: Myocardium is a permanent tissue, so the left ventricle cannot add contractile units by dividing myocytes; instead each myocyte enlarges by synthesizing more structural proteins and organelles, which is hypertrophy. The boxcar-shaped nuclei themselves indicate nuclear enlargement from increased protein synthesis. Hypertrophy here is a pathologic adaptation to systemic hypertension, and when the stress is excessive or persistent it can progress to myocardial injury and heart failure (significant left ventricular hypertrophy leads to myocardial injury leads to heart failure).

explanation_incorrect.B: An increase in cell number by stem cell proliferation is hyperplasia; mature cardiomyocytes have essentially no replicative capacity, so the ventricular wall cannot thicken this way.
explanation_incorrect.C: Ubiquitin-proteasome degradation of cytoskeletal proteins with reduced protein synthesis is the mechanism of atrophy, which shrinks, rather than thickens, the tissue.
explanation_incorrect.D: Replacement of one mature cell type by another better suited to a stressor is metaplasia, a reprogramming of stem cells seen in epithelia and connective tissue, not in myocardium under a pressure load.
explanation_incorrect.E: Pleomorphism, disordered growth, and loss of tissue orientation describe dysplasia, a precancerous epithelial change that is not a form of adaptation and is not seen in hypertrophied myocardium.

educationalObjective: Hypertrophy is an increase in cell size from added structural proteins and organelles, and is the only means by which permanent tissues such as myocardium can respond to increased workload.

subject: Pathology
vignette: A 24-year-old woman, gravida 2, presents at 34 weeks of gestation. Her uterus is markedly enlarged and the fundal height exceeds dates, but the fetus is normally grown and no mass is found. Imaging shows a diffusely thickened myometrium with an increased number of smooth muscle cells and an increased uterine mass. She remains asymptomatic throughout the pregnancy.
question: Which of the following best describes the uterine enlargement in this patient?

options.text: Physiologic hyperplasia and hypertrophy in response to hormonal stimulation
Pathologic hyperplasia that requires evaluation for malignant transformation
Metaplasia of myometrial smooth muscle into a more distensible cell type
An irreversible loss of myometrial cells balanced by fibrotic replacement
Neoplastic clonal expansion of a single smooth muscle cell

explanation_correct: Cellular adaptations can be physiologic as well as pathologic: the classic example of physiologic adaptation is uterine enlargement during pregnancy. In the uterus both hyperplasia (an increased number of smooth muscle cells and stem cell derivatives under hormonal drive) and hypertrophy (enlarged individual smooth muscle cells) contribute, and the change reverses after delivery. Because it is a controlled, appropriate response to a normal stimulus, it is not considered pathologic and does not require work-up for malignancy.

explanation_incorrect.A: Pathologic hyperplasia (for example, endometrial hyperplasia) results from excessive or inappropriate stimulation and may progress to dysplasia and carcinoma, so it requires evaluation; the gravid uterus represents controlled response to normal hormonal stimulation.
explanation_incorrect.B: Metaplasia is replacement of one differentiated cell type by another after reprogramming of stem cells, typically due to an irritant such as gastric acid or tobacco smoke; it does not produce the diffuse myometrial thickening of pregnancy.
explanation_incorrect.C: Loss of cells with fibrotic replacement describes atrophy with scarring (as in a chronically ischemic organ), which would decrease rather than increase uterine mass.
explanation_incorrect.E: Clonal neoplastic expansion of a single cell describes a leiomyoma or leiomyosarcoma, which forms a discrete mass rather than the diffuse, stimulus-driven enlargement of pregnancy.

educationalObjective: Uterine enlargement in pregnancy is the classic physiologic example of combined hyperplasia and hypertrophy, whereas myocardial hypertrophy from hypertension is the classic pathologic example.

subject: Pathology
vignette: A 71-year-old man presents with nocturia, urinary hesitancy, and a weak stream. Digital rectal examination reveals a symmetrically enlarged, rubbery, nontender prostate. Serum prostate-specific antigen is mildly elevated. A biopsy shows nodules of proliferated glands lined by two cell layers with no atypia and no infiltrative growth pattern.
question: Which of the following best characterizes the enlargement of this organ?

options.text: Hypertrophy of prostatic glandular cells with no change in cell number
Hyperplasia with increased numbers of cells within the gland
Metaplasia of prostatic epithelium into stratified squamous epithelium
Atrophy of the transition zone with compensatory stromal scarring
Dysplasia of the prostatic epithelium with loss of nuclear uniformity

explanation_correct: Benign prostatic hyperplasia is the standard example of hyperplasia: controlled proliferation of stem cells and differentiated cells produces an increased number of cells, here forming a nodular, enlarged transition zone that obstructs the urethra. Because the proliferation is controlled and the two cell layers are retained, it is a benign, largely age-related process rather than a malignant one. Hyperplasia is a change in cell number, in contrast to hypertrophy, which is an increase in cell size.

explanation_incorrect.A: Pure hypertrophy would enlarge individual cells without increasing their number; the nodular increase in glandular elements with increased cell count is by definition hyperplasia, and the two adaptations often coexist with hyperplasia predominating here.
explanation_incorrect.C: Metaplasia of the prostatic epithelium into stratified squamous epithelium is not the mechanism of benign prostatic hyperplasia and is not part of that histology; the lesion is glandular proliferation.
explanation_incorrect.D: Atrophy would decrease organ mass with reduced cell size and number, exactly opposite to the enlargement and obstruction described.
explanation_incorrect.E: Dysplasia is disordered, precancerous growth with pleomorphism, increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, and loss of orientation; the biopsy shows benign glands with a preserved two-cell layer and no atypia.

educationalObjective: Benign prostatic hyperplasia is the classic example of hyperplasia, an increase in cell number through controlled proliferation rather than an increase in cell size.

subject: Pathology
vignette: A 54-year-old woman with obesity and chronic anovulation presents with several months of irregular heavy vaginal bleeding. Endometrial biopsy shows crowded glands with an increased number of glandular cells and abundant mitoses but no infiltrative growth. Her clinician explains that if the excessive hormonal stimulation persists, this change can progress to dysplasia and cancer.
question: Which of the following best describes the type of hyperplasia in this patient and its significance?

options.text: Physiologic hyperplasia that will regress without intervention
Hypertrophy of endometrial cells without an increase in cell number
Pathologic hyperplasia that may progress to dysplasia and cancer
Metaplasia of endometrial epithelium to a cell type adapted to estrogen
Apoptosis-driven loss of endometrial cells with cystic dilation of glands

explanation_correct: Excessive stimulation of a proliferative epithelium produces pathologic hyperplasia, and endometrial hyperplasia from unopposed estrogen is the classic First Aid example. Unlike controlled physiologic hyperplasia, pathologic hyperplasia is a change in cell type and structure that carries a risk of progression to dysplasia and eventually carcinoma if the stimulation persists. This is why hyperplasia of the endometrium must be treated or surveilled rather than simply observed.

explanation_incorrect.A: Physiologic hyperplasia, such as that of the pregnant uterus or the lactating breast, is an appropriate response to a normal stimulus and regresses when the stimulus is removed; unopposed estrogen is excessive, not physiologic.
explanation_incorrect.B: Hypertrophy increases cell size without increasing number, but the biopsy shows an increased number of glandular cells with mitoses, which indicates hyperplasia.
explanation_incorrect.D: Metaplasia is a change in cell type after stem cell reprogramming, typically from an irritant such as gastric acid or tobacco smoke; the endometrial epithelium remains endometrial here, only overgrown.
explanation_incorrect.E: Apoptosis removes cells and would reduce endometrial mass; the prolonged bleeding is caused by exuberant, disordered proliferation rather than by apoptotic loss.

educationalObjective: Pathologic hyperplasia from excessive stimulation (for example, unopposed estrogen in the endometrium) can progress to dysplasia and cancer, unlike physiologic hyperplasia.
